en: He did not do what was right.
Though I stayed six years,
He did not acknowledge my service;
He did not ask, 'How did you come here?'
That friend of mine, Kökchö—
His conduct gave the body no comfort,
Nor did his ways gladden the soul.
Always in his home,
He would lie sprawled out.
Bored and weary of idleness,
Taking hero Mazhik along,
Almambet would go scouting.
I would scout sixty river valleys.
For six months, seven months, without returning,
I would go far away.
I traveled on expeditions at ease.
Sixty bears and forty tigers,
The two of us shot,
And to Aydarkan's Kökchö,
Tying them up, we gave them as tribute.
While I was out scouting,
My polished musket hung around my neck.
Not merely over China, but over the world,
'I shall make Kökchö khan,'
Was always in my thoughts.
Then I also went on thinking:
'Outer Beijing and Inner Beijing—
I shall reach them and wage war.
At the very least, Kökchö
I shall make a great lord in Outer Beijing,
And raise him up as khan.'
He had listened to gossip.
'He is my wife's lover,' he thought,
Harboring wicked suspicions.
When I returned from scouting,
In hero Kökchö's encampment
The people stood seething like a cauldron;
A great, sprawling army stood there.
When I saw the great army,
Unable to ride onward, I wandered.
'What times have come?' I thought,
Amazed, unable to understand.
Turning toward Mazhik,
Standing bewildered, I said:
'My true companion from the beginning,
The God who strikes us must have struck!
A dark calamity must have come from Beijing
And pressed down upon him,
Scattering his four kinds of livestock.
When we went away scouting,
With no one to give him support,
They must have plundered Kökchö
And raided him in Sary-Arka.
The army has gathered—
While we were away on the distant hunt,
The enemy must have brought humiliation.
While we were away on the distant hunt,
They must have tormented the Kazakhs,
Their girls and their wives
They must have seized by force!
If the enemy came from Mecca,
Let us bring calamity upon them.
If the enemy came from Beijing,
Let us confront them and fight.
My friend, champion Kökchö,
Let us free him from his suffering
And rescue him.
Whatever it may be,
Come, Mazhik, my mighty one,
Let us go to the great army!”
Saying this to Mazhik,
Aydarkan's Kökchö,
I drew near his camp.
When I approached his camp,
My friend's wife Akerkech,
Taking a scarf in her hand,
Swaying as she stepped and turned,
Came out before me sobbing.
Striding, waving her hand:
“My young friend, stop!” she said,
Calling wretched me.
“Turn your horse's head aside,
Wait on the ground ahead,
Turn your courser aside,
Turn and wait a little!
There is no shame in grave words.
When you went on the hunting expedition,
‘They share one mind and thought,’ he said.
When you went on the hunting expedition,
Aydarkan's Kökchö
Called the two of us lovers,
‘Close together, mingled like dough,’ he said,
Calling the two of us intimates.
Gathering all his people,
He is raising a great uproar.
He showed me many marvels,
Making me see what I had never seen,
He beat me though I was guiltless,
Binding my hands.
When you went on the hunting expedition,
He soaked my dress in blood.
He drove sheep in a stream over me.
When you went on the hunting expedition,
He had me shut in darkness,
Had me beaten time after time.
The Kazakhs gathered and took vengeance,
Made their pledge firm,
Swore to kill us.
First to seize you,
To seize and finish you,
Then me myself,
To gouge out one of my eyes,
To stretch out the strands of my hair,
To give me a letter of divorce,
To slit my soles and put in salt,
To put ice upon my chest,
To dress me in a felt cloak,
To set me on a dark-bay filly,
To my father Karakan's city,
To whip and drive me away:
They made their pledge firm.
Oh, son, leave without contending with the Kazakhs,
Leave without being caught in torment!
Think, son, hear my words!
Leave without entering the palace
Of the black-hearted Kazakh.
Let me take your troubles upon myself,
Leave without drinking what he gives!
If into Khan Kökchö's house
You dismount, oh, son,
There is grain beer in a leather bucket.
Inside that grain beer
There is burning poison too.
In warrior Kökchö's house
There is grain beer in a wooden tub.
Somehow to seize you,
There is a potent poisonous drug mixed in.
Do not weaken by drinking his beer,
Do not meet with many illnesses!
In Khan Kökchö's place of honor,
Bearskin and white bedding:
Upon them, son,
Do not sit at all, son.
Underneath he has dug a pit.
Leave without contending with Kökchö;
He has many Kazakh slaves.
Having fallen to Khan Kökchö,
Wretched me, I have misfortune;
Your sister-in-law has many answers.
For six years he cherished you,
Thinking you his very eye,
The oath has struck you down,
Clasping hands, becoming friends,
The oath has struck your friend down.
Do not turn Sarala's head back,
Toward Kökchö with his wicked thoughts,
Do not keep looking longingly.
If you journey onward from here,
If you travel far without sparing your horse,
Turning where the mountains end,
If you turn to your left,
There lies a truly excellent land,
There are a people fully flourishing.
Ruling those people,
Governing them since long ago,
There is the accomplished warrior Koshoy.
His wide eyes like the morning star,
His great ears like shields,
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan,
Now his wish has been granted,
Now his age has reached seventy,
Now his head rests on a pillow.
Since old age has confronted him,
He has lain down at this time.
Since Koshoy has lain down,
The brow has lost its eyebrows;
The teeming people have lost their head.
The people remaining behind him,
Unable to bear one another,
Not heeding one another's words,
Chattering like jackdaws,
All gathering together,
Have all mounted their horses.
Falling into disorder,
Each now rules his own camp.
Since their elder has become such,
Since their people have become such,
Do not look to that people.
They are not the ones to welcome you;
It is no place to restore your laughter.
When you pass beyond them,
Alty-Shaar, Margalang,
At the far end Bukhara, Samarkand,
In the valley between,
Kokand and Andijan,
Those would be their lands.
Let me tell you their ways:
Round bread big as a hoe tied at their waists,
Opening their mouths toward the sky,
Shouting like madmen.
Do not stay among these people;
It is no place for you to remain,
No people who will welcome you.
Turning to your right,
Traveling over Orolmo-Too,
Crossing many of its ridges,
You will reach broad Talas.
Let me tell you about Talas:
It has marshes tucked in hollow after hollow.
Pecking one another's feathers from their numbers,
Its geese turn as they fly.
To the east and to the west,
Creatures fill its land and water.
Wild sheep bleat on the hills,
Nightingales sing in white willows,
Stags bellow in the brush,
Hinds rest chewing in sheltered places.
Its boars go hunched,
Its snakes go winding,
Its insects bustle,
Its ants teem.
Storks stand stiffly upright,
Its fish eagles stare fiercely.
When you look there,
Storks stand with necks erect.
Broad Talas, better than other lands,
Dwelling in broad Talas
Is the leopard, blood-drinking warrior Manas.
Let me tell you about Manas:
His whole world is in balance;
He is a warrior of extraordinary strength,
A lion supported by holy spirits.
His heart is wider than a lake.
If you settle beside Manas,
He is the warrior who will understand your mind.
If you heed my words, oh, son,
Go and settle in Talas,
Become a companion-warrior to Manas!
If you go there, warrior Manas,
His deeds comfort the soul,
His ways bring the soul delight.
He is the warrior who will ease your troubled heart;
Those are the people who will restore your laughter.
If you grow bored, you will shoot roe deer.
If you are not bored, in Talas
You will play the knucklebone game.
Oh, son, to that blue-maned Manas
A companion-warrior came without a wife.
For the warrior who came without a wife,
A crimson dress, a slender waist,
A beauty among girls, a crescent waist,
Having his people judge her,
Having them choose without tiring,
Warrior Manas obtained her for him.
For the companion who came without a coat,
Golden collar, copper sleeves,
